paper.title_en: Sideband-mediated nuclear-spin-wave memory for an Andreev spin qubit: required coherence and Floquet feasibility
paper.abstract_en: We propose and quantitatively analyze a Floquet-driven red-sideband architecture that couples an Andreev spin qubit (ASQ) in a semiconductor Josephson junction to a collective nuclear spin-wave memory, and we establish the coherence and calibration requirements an experiment would need to meet. Frequency modulation of the ASQ transition bridges its GHz frequency to the MHz nuclear Larmor frequency, giving an effective sideband coupling $g_{\mathrm{eff}} = g_{\mathrm{mg}}J_1(\beta)$ with modulation index $\beta = \Omega_\mathrm d/\omega_\mathrm d$. For a single-isotope $ ^{75}$As ($I = 3/2$) bright mode over $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 10^{5}$-$10^{6}$ nuclei, two explicit parameter sets give $g_{\mathrm{eff}}/2\pi$ in the 9-367 kHz range and SWAP times of 0.7-28 $\mu$s. The central result is a required-coherence map: a high-fidelity write-read cycle (two-SWAP survival $F_{\mathrm{WR}}\gtrsim 0.9$, memory number $\mathcal{M}\equiv 2\pi(g_{\mathrm{eff}}/2\pi)T_{2,\mathrm{ASQ}}\gtrsim 30$) needs $T_{2,\mathrm{ASQ}}\sim 13$-$520\;\mu$s, whereas currently demonstrated ASQ coherences ($\sim 10$-$100$ ns) lie two to five orders of magnitude below this target. The ASQ coherence time is thus identified as the limiting resource, and sweet-spot operation, phase-bias engineering, and Floquet-dressed protection as the routes to close the gap. A next-order Floquet expansion fixes the calibration budget-dominated by an $n = 0$ Jaynes-Cummings dispersive shift that separates into a static and a weak drive-induced part-and a two-mode stroboscopic Lindblad simulation confirms the required-coherence crossover and bounds the effect of the counter-rotating channel (sub-percent at the baseline, rising to a $2.3$-percentage-point penalty only for worst-case opposite-circular coupling). All coupling values are feasibility estimates set by a few device-specific parameters whose determination from a Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculation is the natural next step.
